title: The Sermon on the Mount
intro: 20 days through the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew 5 to 7, one passage at a time.

posts.caption: Tradition places this sermon on a hillside in Galilee, near the lakeside town of Capernaum. Many readers see Jesus here as a new Moses, teaching from a mountain as Moses brought the Law down from Sinai. "Blessed" translates the Greek makarios, which also means "happy" or "fortunate." Starting today, 20 days through the Sermon on the Mount, Matthew chapters 5 to 7.

These sayings are called the Beatitudes, from the Latin beatus, "blessed." Each pairs an unlikely group of people with a promise from God. The line about the meek echoes Psalm 37:11. Luke records a shorter version of this sermon, often called the Sermon on the Plain (Luke 6), with four blessings followed by four warnings.

Three more Beatitudes, about mercy, a pure heart, and making peace. In Hebrew idiom, being a "son of" something meant sharing its character, so "sons of God" suggests people who resemble God. The list closes with blessings on those persecuted for doing right. The name "Sermon on the Mount" goes back to a commentary Augustine wrote in the 390s.

From blessings, Jesus turns to what his followers are for. Salt was valuable in the ancient world, used to preserve food as well as flavor it. Pure salt can't lose its taste, but many scholars think local salt, mixed with other minerals, could turn bland. "Salt of the earth" became an English phrase for good, honest people.

Ancient towns were often built on hills, and their lights could be seen from far away at night. In 1630 the Puritan leader John Winthrop borrowed this image for the colony he hoped to build in New England, and later US presidents, including John F. Kennedy and Ronald Reagan, quoted it. Jesus goes on to say a lamp belongs on a stand, not under a basket.

"The Law and the Prophets" was a way of naming the Hebrew scriptures. Jesus says he hasn't come to set them aside, and adds that not one "jot" will disappear: the yod, the smallest letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Christians have discussed what he means by "fulfill" ever since.

Six times in this chapter Jesus sets what "was said" beside "But I tell you." Here he quotes "eye for eye" from the Torah, a law many scholars see as limiting revenge to equal measure, and goes further. Roman soldiers could force civilians to carry their gear, which may lie behind the "one mile." Leo Tolstoy and Mahatma Gandhi both drew on this teaching in their thinking on nonviolence.

The last of the six "But I tell you" sayings. "Love your neighbor" comes from Leviticus 19:18, but "hate your enemy" appears nowhere in the Hebrew scriptures; Jesus may be quoting a popular way of reading it. His reason is God's own generosity, with sun and rain for everyone. Martin Luther King Jr. preached a well-known sermon on this passage, "Loving Your Enemies."

Chapter 6 covers three practices of Jewish devotion: giving to the poor, prayer, and fasting. For each one, Jesus warns against doing it to be seen and admired. The "inner room" was a private storeroom; older English Bibles called it a "closet," which gave rise to the phrase "prayer closet."

posts.display: So then, this is how you should pray: ‘Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.’
posts.caption: The Lord's Prayer, the best-known prayer in Christianity, which Jesus gives as a model. Luke records a shorter version in Luke 11. "Hallowed" is an old English word meaning honored as holy. The prayer begins with God's name, kingdom, and will before it turns to everyday needs.

posts.display: ‘Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.’
posts.caption: The second half of the Lord's Prayer asks for bread, forgiveness, and protection. Matthew's word is "debts," a common image for sins, though many churches pray "trespasses." The familiar ending, "For thine is the kingdom...," is missing from the oldest manuscripts of Matthew; it was likely added for use in worship, and many churches still pray it.

In the ancient world, wealth was often kept as fine clothing, stored grain, or coins, all open to moths, decay, and theft. Thieves could dig through the walls of many ancient houses, and the Greek word for "break in" literally means "dig through." Jesus contrasts that fragile wealth with treasure "in heaven," and ends with a saying about where the heart follows.

Jesus turns to worry. He points to the birds and, next, to the wildflowers, the "lilies of the field," which outshine King Solomon in all his glory. The argument moves from lesser to greater, a common style of Jewish teaching: if God cares for birds and flowers, how much more for people.

The last line of Jesus' teaching on worry. Just before it comes one of the sermon's best-known sayings: seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added. This closing line has a practical, almost proverbial ring.

Chapter 7 opens with one of the most quoted lines in the Bible. The "measure" was a container for measuring grain in the marketplace, and the image is of getting back what you hand out. Jesus follows it with a picture many readers find deliberately comic: someone with a wooden beam in his own eye, trying to remove a speck from his brother's.

Three images for prayer, each with a promise. The Greek verbs are in a tense that suggests continuing action: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking. Jesus goes on to compare God to a father who would never hand his child a stone when asked for bread.

This is known as the Golden Rule, and similar sayings appear in many cultures. Shortly before Jesus' time, the famous Jewish teacher Hillel summed up the Torah in a negative form: don't do to others what is hateful to you. Jesus states it positively, and like Hillel he presents it as the heart of the scriptures.

The sermon's ending is built on contrasts: two gates, two kinds of trees, two builders. The picture of two ways, one leading to life and one to destruction, is an old one in Jewish teaching, found in Deuteronomy and Psalm 1. An early Christian handbook, the Didache, also begins with "two ways."

The sermon ends with a short parable. In Galilee, dry stream beds could flood suddenly in the rainy season. Both builders hear the same words; the difference is whether they act on them. When the storm comes, the house on the rock stands, while the house on sand falls with a great crash.

The crowd's reaction as the sermon ends. Many scholars think the scribes, the teachers of the law, mostly taught by citing earlier authorities, while Jesus spoke on his own: "But I tell you." Matthew closes each of the five big teaching sections of his Gospel with a line like this one. That's the whole Sermon on the Mount. Thank you for reading it with me.
